coachMessages.text: Yellow has a threat up in that column. How safe is it? Count the empty cells between the column top and the threat cell.

slides.infoProse:
<board instructions>Show a column (any column) that is partially empty, with Yellow having a horizontal major threat at some cell in that column. The column top should be at least 3 empty cells below the threat cell. Place a `tg` overlay on the threat cell and `td` overlays on each of the 3 empty gap cells between the column top and the threat. The rest of the board should have enough discs to make a plausible mid-game position.</board instructions>

A Z-Threat is a major threat where the number of empty cells from the current column top up to and including the threat cell is odd. Count those cells — that number is all you need.

coachMessages.text: You enter this column first. You go 1st, opponent 2nd, you 3rd — and you land on the threat. But this only works if you are the one to play into the column first.

slides.infoProse:
<board instructions>Same column and threat as slide 1. Use alternating `tg` / `td` overlays on the gap cells to show the turn sequence: first gap cell = `tg` (your move), second = `td` (opponent), threat cell = `tg` (your move). The alternation should make it visually clear that you land on the threat.</board instructions>

With 3 empty cells you play moves 1 and 3 in this column; your opponent plays move 2. Since 3 is odd, the last move — the threat cell — is yours. That is what makes it a Z-Threat.

Critical condition: **you must be the one to enter the column first.** If your opponent plays into this column before you, the sequence reverses — they play moves 1 and 3, and they land on your threat cell instead.

coachMessages.text: Now the gap is 2. You go 1st, opponent goes 2nd — and lands on your threat cell. Even gap means the threat doesn't work yet.

slides.infoProse:
<board instructions>Same setup as slides 1–2 but change the gap to 2 cells (even). Mark the first gap cell `tg` (your move) and the threat cell `td` (opponent's move — they land there). The threat cell should visually signal 'not yours'.</board instructions>

Even gap: 2 empty cells, you play 1st, opponent plays 2nd and reaches the threat. This is not a Z-Threat — entering the column first hands the threat cell to your opponent. You need an odd gap for the threat to be yours.

coachMessages.text: The column already has discs. Don't count from the bottom — count from the top of the stack. The stack shifts the parity.

slides.infoProse:
<board instructions>Show a column that is already partially filled (2–3 discs at the bottom). Yellow has a horizontal threat above the stack. The raw row number of the threat should be even (a naive student using row parity would say 'not mine'), but the gap from the stack top to the threat should be odd (1 or 3). Mark the gap cells `td` and the threat cell `tg`. This is the key gotcha: count from the stack top, not from row 0.</board instructions>

The raw row number can mislead you. What matters is the gap from the current column top to the threat cell. Even an 'even-row' threat becomes a Z-Threat if the discs below it shift the count to odd. Always count from the stack top.

socratic._boardInstructions: Show a mid-game position where Yellow has a horizontal major threat at row 2 in two different columns: column 3 and one other column (e.g., column 6). Column 3 already has exactly one disc at the bottom (row 0), so the gap from the column top to the threat is 1 cell (odd) — making it a Z-Threat. The distractor column is fully empty, so its gap to row 2 is 2 cells (even) — not a Z-Threat. Mark Yellow's threat cell in column 3 with 'tg' and the threat cell in the distractor column with 'td'. The student must notice that the single disc in column 3 shifts the parity — the same row number, opposite ownership.

confirmationChallenges.goalPrompt: Identify the column where a Z-threat gives you unstoppable parity control.
